faqs.answer: Yellow leaves usually point to excess moisture around the roots, poor drainage, or a sudden environmental change. Check for soggy soil, root stress, and lower light. Early correction is important when caring for fiddleleaf fig.
faqs.question: Why are my fiddleleaf fig leaves turning yellow?

faqs.answer: It usually performs more predictably indoors in bright rooms, where temperature and humidity stay steadier. Outdoors, it grows best only in warm, frost-free climates with sheltered conditions and filtered sun.
faqs.question: Does fiddleleaf fig grow better indoors or outdoors?

faqs.answer: Yes. As roots fill the pot, growth may slow, the soil may dry faster, and the plant can become top-heavy. For stable fiddleleaf fig indoor care, move it to a slightly larger container when rootbound.
faqs.question: Can fiddleleaf fig outgrow its container?

cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep Ficus lyrata tidy and healthy.
bullets: Every 4–8 weeks, remove spent leaves and damaged growth to reduce stress and improve appearance.
Shorten leggy stems back to a node with clean, disinfected pruners to encourage denser growth.

support.intro: Ficus lyrata may need light support as it grows upright indoors.
bullets: Check ties and stake firmness every 4–6 weeks.
Loosen tight ties to prevent stem damage.
Guide leaning new growth back toward the stake.

aeration.intro: Light aeration helps if the topsoil becomes compacted.
bullets: Every 6–8 weeks, gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) with a stick or small fork.
Aerate sooner if water sits on the surface or the soil hardens between waterings.

cleaning.intro: Clean foliage and the pot area every 2–4 weeks.
bullets: Wipe leaves gently with a soft damp cloth, supporting each leaf to avoid tearing.
Remove fallen debris and rinse the saucer or pot exterior to reduce pest shelter and salt buildup.
Clean leaves absorb light better and keep the plant looking neat.

humidity.intro: Humidity support is only sometimes needed for this plant indoors.
bullets: Check weekly in dry rooms. Use a pebble tray or humidifier as needed, and watch for brown leaf edges as a sign of low humidity.

mulching.intro: Mulching is optional but useful for indoor Ficus lyrata.
bullets: Refresh a 1–2 cm (0.4–0.8 in) layer of bark fines or coco chips every 3–4 months.
This top dressing helps slow surface drying and buffers root-zone temperature swings.

watering.intro: Water the fiddleleaf fig on a simple repeating schedule.
bullets: About every 5 days, water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves start to droop slightly.
Soak the soil fully until water runs from the drainage holes, then empty the saucer so roots do not sit in water.
Avoid the common mistake of watering by calendar alone when the soil is still wet.

fertilize.intro: Feed fiddleleaf fig regularly during active growth.
bullets: Apply a balanced houseplant fertilizer at 1/2 strength every 2–4 weeks in spring and summer.
Add fertilizer to moist soil after watering, not to dry roots, for gentler uptake.
Pause or reduce feeding in autumn and winter, and avoid overfeeding, which can burn roots.

repotting.intro: Check repotting needs regularly to avoid root stress.
bullets: Inspect every 6–12 months for roots circling or emerging from drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through.
If needed, move up 1 pot size, about 5–8 cm (2–3 in) wider, using a well-draining chunky mix.

inspection.intro: Do a closer hands-on inspection every 2–4 weeks.
bullets: Lift and check leaf undersides, the stem base, and drainage holes for pests, damage, or excess moisture.
Look for root crowding at the holes or a tight root mass; act if you find pests, mushy stem tissue, or circling roots.

monitoring.intro: Do a quick visual review each week.
bullets: Look at leaf color and texture, new growth, soil moisture, and any visible pest activity.
If leaves dull, soften, spot, or growth stalls, adjust light or watering and inspect more closely at the next care task.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Ficus lyrata is a tropical ornamental tree grown indoors for its large, upright leaves and bold, sculptural shape. It usually grows as a single-stemmed houseplant and can become tall with age.

This species is native to western Africa, where it grows in warm, bright conditions. Its broad leaves give it strong visual appeal, but they also show stress quickly when light, moisture, or placement is inconsistent.

For anyone learning how to care for fiddleleaf fig, the main challenge is keeping conditions steady. It prefers bright, indirect light, slightly moist soil, and a well-draining mix.

careAdvice.title: Rotate Gradually
careAdvice.description: Turn the pot 90° every 1–2 weeks during active growth so the canopy develops evenly, but avoid sudden changes in position because this species often reacts by dropping leaves.

careAdvice.title: Clean Large Leaves
careAdvice.description: Wipe the leaves with a damp soft cloth every 2–4 weeks to remove dust, which improves light capture and makes early spider mite or scale problems easier to spot when caring for fiddleleaf fig.

careAdvice.title: Stake Young Stems
careAdvice.description: Use a soft tie and a slim stake for top-heavy or leaning young plants, checking ties every few months so the stem stays upright without being constricted as it thickens.

careAdvice.title: Inspect New Growth
careAdvice.description: Check the undersides of new leaves and along the midrib weekly for thrips, scale, and spider mites, since early infestations are much easier to control when growing fiddleleaf fig indoors.

soil.intro: Ficus lyrata needs an airy, moisture-retentive mix that drains quickly.
bullets: Use a loamy, organic-rich houseplant mix with chunky structure rather than dense, fine soil.
Blend potting mix with pine bark and perlite; a little coarse sand can further improve drainage.
Aim for slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0–7.0.
Avoid heavy clay-like mixes or compacted media that stay wet and limit root aeration.

water.intro: Keep the soil slightly moist, not wet.
bullets: Water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry, rather than by a fixed schedule; many plants need water about every 5 days in active growth.
Reduce watering in cooler, darker months, and use a potting mix with strong drainage so excess water moves through quickly.
Overwatering shows as yellowing leaves, soft stems, or sour soil; underwatering in Ficus lyrata often causes drooping, dry edges, and leaf drop.

soilPH.intro: A slightly acidic to neutral root zone suits Ficus lyrata best.
bullets: Aim for pH 6.0–7.0, with best growth around mildly acidic to near neutral soil.
Test with a soil meter or kit; raise low pH with small amounts of lime, or lower high pH with sulfur-based amendments.
Wrong pH can cause nutrient lock-out, pale new leaves, interveinal chlorosis, and slower growth even when feeding is adequate.

pruning.intro: Pruning helps Ficus lyrata stay balanced and manageable indoors.
bullets: Prune in spring or early summer, when recovery and new growth are strongest.
Remove dead, damaged, or crowded leaves and weak stems with clean, sharp pruners.
Cut above a node to guide branching and improve shape.
Wear gloves, as the milky sap can irritate skin.

humidity.intro: Humidity matters for fiddleleaf fig and is best kept at 40–60%.
bullets: It tolerates average indoor air but struggles below 30–40% for long periods.
Dry edges, curling, browning, and stalled new growth can indicate humidity stress.
Raise humidity with a pebble tray, nearby humidifier, or grouping, while keeping airflow steady.

sunlight.intro: Bright, indirect light keeps fiddleleaf fig compact and evenly leafy.
bullets: Aim for 6–8 hours daily, ideally filtered light or gentle morning sun.
It tolerates partial shade, but under 4–5 hours often causes slower growth and larger gaps between leaves.
Shield from harsh afternoon sun, especially in summer, as direct exposure can scorch leaves; in winter, move closer to the brightest window or light source.

container.intro: This species grows well in containers when root space, drainage, and stability are managed carefully.
bullets: Use a pot with several drainage holes so excess water leaves quickly after each watering.
Choose a container 25–40 cm (10–16 in) wide and deep enough to anchor the root ball evenly.
For a top-heavy Ficus lyrata, a heavier pot helps prevent tipping and steadies upright growth.

placement.intro: Bright indoor placement suits the fiddleleaf fig best in most homes.
bullets: Grow indoors near an east- or south-facing window with bright, indirect light; outdoors only in warm climates in a bright, sheltered position.
Leave space around the plant for airflow and even light, and rotate it regularly to reduce leaning.
Avoid cold drafts, air conditioner flow, heating vents, and harsh direct midday sun that can scorch leaves.

fertilizer.intro: Light feeding supports steady indoor growth in the fiddleleaf fig.
bullets: Use a balanced NPK houseplant fertilizer or a slow-release formula; compost is less practical indoors.
Feed every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer when growth is active.
Apply at 1/2 strength to reduce salt buildup and root stress.
Reduce or stop feeding in winter when growth slows.

winterCare.intro: Winter care matters because this tropical species is not frost tolerant.
bullets: Keep plants indoors at 18–29°C (64–84°F), away from freezing drafts and cold glass.
Reduce watering slightly, but do not let the soil stay dry for long.
Skip mulch indoors; for containers, insulate the pot only during cold moves.
Maintain bright, indirect light and moderate humidity to limit leaf drop.

propagation.intro: Propagation is possible, though seed is the standard method for Ficus lyrata.
bullets: Sow fresh seeds in spring in a warm, sterile, lightly moist medium.
Keep at 24–29°C (75–84°F) with bright, indirect light and steady humidity.
Cover lightly, allow airflow, and avoid waterlogging during germination.
Transplant seedlings once they are established and handling causes minimal root disturbance.

temperature.intro: Warm, stable temperatures support steady growth.
bullets: Best growth is usually at 65–84°F (18–29°C), with the strongest growth often around 70–80°F (21–27°C).
Avoid prolonged exposure below 55°F (13°C); cold drafts and sudden temperature swings can trigger leaf drop.
Frost can damage or kill this species, and heat above 90°F (32°C) is tolerated better with shade, airflow, and consistent soil moisture.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Container plants benefit from repotting when root space becomes limited.
bullets: Repot in spring or early summer if roots circle the pot, drainage slows, or growth stalls.
Most plants need a larger pot every 1–2 years, moving up 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in).
Use a well-draining chunky mix and a pot with drainage holes.
Water after repotting and keep bright, indirect light while roots settle.

facts.text: In its native West African range, this species can begin life high in another tree and later send roots down to the ground. As it matures, it may behave as a strangler fig, gradually enveloping its host.

facts.text: Its large leaves are the source of the common name fiddle-leaf fig. The species epithet lyrata also refers to a lyre-shaped form, echoing the outline of the leaf blade.
facts.title: Violin-shaped leaves

facts.text: This species has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. That recognition reflects its value as a reliable ornamental plant under suitable growing conditions.

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Like other true figs, this species produces a syconium, a hollow fig structure lined inside with many tiny flowers rather than showing obvious external blooms.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Spider mites
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Wipe both sides of the leaves and rinse the plant thoroughly, then repeat with insecticidal soap or neem-based treatment every 7–10 days until activity stops. Raise humidity to 40–60%, keep the plant away from hot dry drafts, and inspect nearby plants.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects are a frequent indoor problem in dry air and often gather on the undersides of leaves. Symptoms include fine webbing, pale stippling, and gradual leaf yellowing or drop.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Scale insects
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove visible insects with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then wash the plant and follow with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap. Check stems, leaf joints, and undersides weekly, as young crawlers are easier to control than mature scale.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This pest appears as small brown or tan bumps on stems and leaves and feeds on plant sap. Symptoms include sticky residue, weak growth, and yellowing leaves.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Mealybugs
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Isolate the plant, remove clusters by hand with alcohol on a swab, and rinse the foliage well. Repeat treatment with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil every 7–10 days until no new insects appear.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects hide in leaf axils and along stems, where they form white cottony clusters. Symptoms include sticky honeydew, distorted growth, and leaf drop under heavier infestations.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Bacterial leaf spot
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove affected leaves with clean tools and avoid wetting the foliage during watering. Improve air movement, keep leaves dry, and reduce crowding so new growth stays cleaner.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease causes dark, water-soaked or irregular spots that can enlarge and merge, especially when leaves stay wet. Symptoms often worsen in crowded conditions with poor airflow.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Anthracnose
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Prune off affected leaves, discard fallen debris, and keep the plant in bright, indirect light with steady airflow. Water the soil directly rather than the leaves, and avoid overcrowded placement near other plants.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease can cause brown to black lesions on leaves, often starting near edges or damaged tissue. Symptoms may spread faster in warm, humid conditions when moisture remains on the foliage.
